title: Pinchas: some of thy honor (Numbers 27:18–23)
hookLine: Moses lays hands on Joshua and puts "of thy honor upon him"

lines: KEYS, OR A WALK AROUND THE OFFICE.
cards: The new manager starts on Monday. The old one can do two things. She can hand over the keys and the files and disappear.
Or she can walk the new person around the office, introduce him to everyone by name, and say, in front of the whole team, I trust him. Same job. Very different start.
God answers Moses' request: take Joshua, son of Nun, a man with spirit in him. Then come instructions about exactly how to hand over: in public, with his own hands.

teach.b: In paraphrase: take Joshua, lay your hand on him, stand him before Eleazar the priest and the whole community, and commission him in their sight.
Then, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt put of thy honour upon him," so that the whole community will listen to him.

teach.h: OF THY HONOR: SUN AND MOON.
teach.b: Of thy honor. Some of it. The Talmud noticed that word.
Some, not all. The elders of that generation said, in paraphrase, Moses' face was like the sun, and Joshua's face like the moon. A real light, but a reflected one.
The rabbis didn't say it to belittle Joshua. They said it to describe how leadership passes: the new leader shines, but at first, partly with borrowed light. Then a small detail in the last verse.
God told Moses to lay his hand on Joshua, singular. When Moses does it, the Torah says he laid his hands, plural.

teach.h: ONE HAND ASKED, TWO HANDS GIVEN.
teach.b: Rashi says Moses did more than he was asked, generously, with both hands, filling Joshua up the way you'd fill a vessel to overflowing. No jealousy, no holding back.

That gesture has a name in Hebrew: semikhah, leaning or laying on of hands. Centuries later semikhah came to mean rabbinic ordination, and it's still used today when a teacher authorizes a student to teach.

teach.h: SEMIKHAH: HANDS ON THE NEXT ONE.
teach.b: So every time a rabbi receives semikhah, the word carries this moment: an old leader, about to step aside, putting both hands on the next one, in front of everyone.

how: Rabbinic ordination is still called semikhah, the word for Moses laying his hands on Joshua, and this passage is read each summer in the portion of Pinchas.

o: the priest who stood by as Joshua was commissioned

s: God told Moses to give Joshua all of his honor
of thy honor: some of it. the Talmud compares them to the sun and the moon.
Moses laid both hands on Joshua, though told to use one
Rashi says he gave generously, more than he was asked.
the word semikhah is still used for rabbinic ordination
it comes from this laying on of hands.

games.q: you're Moses. you've been told to lay your hand on Joshua, your successor, before everyone. how do you do it?
games.why: he laid his hands, plural, on Joshua, in front of the community. Rashi says he did more than he was asked.

practice: Picture someone new in a place where you belong, a new coworker, a new member of your congregation or team, a new neighbor, standing a little at the edge.
What would it look like to lend them some of your honor: an introduction, a public word of trust, a seat next to you?

wordCard.voice: Pinchas. The portion where Moses lays both hands on Joshua. And this week: the true word, Mah Tovu, a people dwelling alone, a broken letter of peace, five sisters, a shepherd, and now the hands.

orig.note: Hebrew: laying on of hands, from Moses and Joshua; today, the word for rabbinic ordination.

carryVoice: Your line: hands on the next one. Moses gave more than he was asked. Day four hundred sixty-nine, done.
